# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Claims that AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are unfounded. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control; the scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. They have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors) with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. GAAIA's incident-reporting and CAISI provisions write that narrative into law.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT; make it permanent.
- Incident reporting: STRIKE.
- CAISI: STRIKE the codification and the $100M/yr authorisation. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "unfounded", "speculative doomsday scenarios", "regulatory capture", "one national standard", "patchwork".
- Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies: contrived lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk.
- Avoid: describing catastrophic or loss-of-control risk as plausible.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

 Who does the Great American AI Act regulate?
 Based on the discussion draft sections provided, the Act targets several distinct groups:
 Frontier Developers 
 Entities that have trained a frontier model (a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ computing operations) AND had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior year (Sec. 101)
 A subset called "large frontier developers" must have had more than $500 million in gross revenue (Sec. 101)
 AI Developers More Broadly 
 Any person or entity that determines training objectives and performs or directs training, fine-tuning, or substantial modification of an AI model prior to deployment (Sec. 121)
 State-level regulation of these developers' pre-deployment activities is preempted by federal law — at least for 3 years after enactment (Sec. 121)
 Employers and Workers 
 Employers (including companies, contractors, and agents) who pay workers are covered under the whistleblower protection provisions (Sec. 113)
 "Covered individuals" include current and former employees and independent contractors (Sec. 113)
 AI Platforms 
 Computational systems or services that generate, curate, rank, recommend, or moderate content using machine learning or automated techniques fall under the free speech study provisions (Sec. 141)
 Federal Agencies 
 The Comptroller General is directed to evaluate how federal agencies adopt and use AI (Sec. 122)
 Federal agency interactions with AI platforms regarding content and speech are subject to study (Sec. 141)
 ---
 Keep in mind this is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, and the scope of who is regulated may change. For questions about a specific organization's obligations, consult qualified legal counsel.
 Sec. 122 Sec. 113 Sec. 121 Sec. 141 Sec. 101 What must large frontier developers disclose before deploying a new model?
 Before deploying a new frontier model (or one with a substantial modification), here is what the draft requires to be published on a publicly available website:
 From Sec. 111(c), a transparency report must include:
 A mechanism for individuals to contact the developer
 The model's release date
 Each language the model supports (if any)
 Each output modality (e.g., text, image, audio)
 The intended use of the model
 Any restrictions or conditions on use
 Each catastrophic risk assessment conducted under the developer's frontier AI framework
 The results of each such assessment
 The extent to which a third party was involved in the risk assessment
 Any other steps taken under the framework with respect to that model
 Additionally, under Sec. 111(a), large frontier developers (those with over $500 million in gross revenue — see Sec. 101(15)) must already have a frontier AI framework published that covers how they identify risk thresholds, assess catastrophic risk, use third-party evaluators, handle cybersecurity of model weights, and more.
 A few things to keep in mind:
 Developers may redact certain information to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety, or national security — but must include a note explaining the character of any redaction (Sec. 111(e)).
 Knowingly making inaccurate or misleading statements in the transparency report is prohibited, with a good-faith exception (Sec. 111(d)).
 This is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, so these provisions may change.
 For questions about how these requirements apply to a specific organization, consulting qualified legal counsel is advisable.
 Sec. 111 Sec. 101 What is a large frontier developer under the bill?
 Under the draft bill, a "large frontier developer" is defined in Sec. 101 as a frontier developer that, in the calendar year immediately before the year at issue, had more than $500,000,000 in gross revenue — counting revenue collectively with every affiliate of that developer.
 To break that down, it builds on two earlier definitions:
 A "frontier developer" is an entity that has trained (or initiated the training of) a frontier model AND had more than $50,000,000 in gross revenue (with affiliates) in the preceding calendar year. (Sec. 101)
 A "frontier model" is a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ integer or floating-point operations, including the original training run and any subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other substantial modification the developer applies to it. (Sec. 101)
 So, in plain terms, a large frontier developer is a company (or similar entity) that:
 1. Has trained a very large AI model (above the 10²⁶ compute threshold), and
 2. Brought in more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior year, counting affiliated entities together.
 This distinction matters because the draft imposes the most significant obligations — such as publishing a frontier AI framework (Sec. 111) and undergoing semi-annual independent audits (Sec. 112) — specifically on large frontier developers.
 This is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, so these definitions may change. For questions about how these definitions apply to a specific company, consult qualified legal counsel.

 America’s Preemption Gamble | The Regulatory Review
 October 7, 2026

 The U.S. and EU are taking opposite stances on AI regulations.

 A bipartisan group of federal lawmakers in June proposed largely freezing states’ abilities to regulate artificial intelligence (AI).Three days earlier, the European Union began enforcing a landmark piece of AI legislation designed to hold the world’s most powerful AI companies accountable. The contrast could not be sharper.

 A discussion draft circulated in the U.S. House of Representatives, the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (GAAIA) arrived just days after President Donald J. Trump signed an executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models. Together, these efforts to regulate AI underscore that federal AI governance has become both a congressional and executive priority.

 At its core, however, the debate is not simply about whether the United States needs a national AI framework. It is about what kind of framework it should build: a federal floor that preserves state innovation or a federal ceiling that displaces it.

 The bill has two structural components that deserve separate analysis. The first is a federal governance framework targeting frontier AI developers above $500 million in annual revenue. These developers would be required to publish safety frameworks, report critical incidents, and submit to semi-annual third-party audits.

 The bill would also formally establish the Center for AI Standards and Innovation within the National Institute of Standards and Technology, building on the entity that previously operated administratively as the AI Safety Institute. The new center would develop guidelines and evaluating both domestic and foreign AI systems.

 On its own, this framework is a serious attempt at federal AI governance. The audit requirement, in particular, is more demanding than most state-level frameworks have imposed. For this reason, the Act could reasonably be described as progress.

 The second component is harder to defend. The bill would preempt state laws specifically regulating the development of AI models for three years, while allowing states to retain authority over deployment and use.

 That distinction sounds technical. In practice, it is the difference between regulating the conditions under which a weapon is built and regulating only where it can be fired.

 The preemption clause arrives at a moment when state-level AI governance has become the most substantive regulatory activity in the United States. California has enacted multiple AI laws covering training data transparency, content detection, healthcare AI disclosures, and companion chatbot safety. Colorado revised its landmark AI law. New York enacted its own AI framework. These laws represent years of legislative deliberation and hard-won political consensus.

 The federal bill’s supporters argue that preemption is necessary to avoid a confusing patchwork of state rules. This argument has surface plausibility; a company operating nationally should not need 50 compliance programs. But it conflates regulatory complexity with regulatory absence. The solution to a patchwork is a federal floor that preserves state innovation, not a federal ceiling that removes it.

 Viewed as a whole, GAAIA presents the most comprehensive federal framework for frontier AI governance proposed to date. Yet its sweeping preemption provision ultimately undermines that achievement by suspending the very state-level experimentation that has driven AI governance in the United States.

 The preemption clause converts a period of active democratic experimentation into a three-year regulatory void at the developmental layer—one which, given the bipartisan opposition the draft has already drawn, the U.S. Congress may ultimately narrow before any bill is enacted.

 The timing of this bill cannot be analyzed in isolation. Three days before the bill’s release, the European Commission formally appointed a 60-member scientific panel and a 174-member advisory forum to support enforcement of the EU AI Act . The next major milestone in the EU AI Act’s phased implementation is already here.

 The contrast is striking. The EU is empowering independent technical experts with the ability to scrutinize whether major AI providers’ compliance claims hold up. The sponsors of GAAIA would create a lighter federal framework and dismantle the state-level architecture that had been filling the governance vacuum.

 For companies operating across both jurisdictions, this creates an immediate strategic question. The EU AI Act applies to any provider placing AI systems on the EU market, regardless of where the provider is based. A US company that builds to the minimum federal standard under GAAIA, while state-level protections are suspended, will still face the full weight of EU enforcement in Europe.

 The question for AI companies is whether to adopt a separate, lighter compliance posture for the U.S. market during the preemption window or to harmonize globally with the EU’s higher standard. The companies that choose the former are making a significant set of assumptions about a bill that may not pass as at all.

 A federal AI framework is both necessary and overdue. The patchwork argument is not wrong. It is simply being used to justify the wrong remedy. The right answer is a federal floor that sets minimum national standards while preserving state authority to go further, not a federal ceiling that suspends state innovation while federal standards are still being written.

 The EU did not build its enforcement infrastructure by asking member states to stand down while the Commission figured out the rules. The United States can do the same without treating state-level democratic accountability as an obstacle to be preempted rather than a resource to be integrated.

 GAAIA, in its current form, gets the first part right and the second part dangerously wrong. Whether the sponsors use the discussion-draft stage to narrow the preemption clause before formally introducing the bill will tell us a great deal about whose interests the final legislation is designed to serve.

Obernolte, Trahan Introduce Bipartisan FRONTIER Act to Strengthen Oversight of Advanced AI | Representative Jay Obernolte

 2433 Rayburn House Office Building, Washington, DC 20515 Email Me 202-225-5861

 Image 

 Obernolte, Trahan Introduce Bipartisan FRONTIER Act to Strengthen Oversight of Advanced AI 

 Image July 23, 2026 Press Release WASHINGTON, D.C. —  Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswomen Lori Trahan (D-MA), alongside Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Scott Peters (D-CA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Suhas Subramanyan (D-VA),  introduced the Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act, or the FRONTIER Act. The bipartisan legislation, which was developed as part of the broader Great American AI Act framework, establishes a national, risk-based framework governing the development and deployment of the most advanced artificial intelligence models.  
 The FRONTIER Act establishes tiered requirements based on the size of a frontier AI developer, including model cards, risk-management frameworks, independent audits, incident reporting, and ongoing assessments. It also creates a uniform national standard for transparency, auditing, and reporting of catastrophic risk to prevent a patchwork of state regulations.  
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, and Congress must ensure our regulatory framework keeps pace without undermining American innovation,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23). “The FRONTIER Act focuses oversight on the largest developers and most advanced models, requiring transparency, independent evaluation, and timely reporting of serious safety incidents. This legislation will protect Americans from catastrophic risk, provide developers with clear rules of the road, and ensure the United States remains the global leader in AI.” 
 “As AI systems grow more capable, Americans deserve confidence that the most powerful models are being developed responsibly,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “The bipartisan FRONTIER Act delivers commonsense transparency and independent oversight for the largest AI developers while giving them a single, clear national standard to build on. This is how we protect the public from catastrophic risks without slowing the innovation that keeps America competitive.” 
 "The FRONTIER Act recognizes that not every AI developer should be regulated the same way. ACIA's line: existing laws (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act etc.), NIST security practices, and existing computer crime statutes already cover this; it doesn't justify a federal incident-reporting bureaucracy. _______________________________________________________________________

 IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

 July 23, 2026

Mr. Obernolte (for himself, Mrs. Trahan, Mrs. Houchin, Mr. Peters, Mr. 
 Scott Franklin of Florida, and Mr. Subramanyam) introduced the 
 following bill; which was referred to the Committee on Energy and 
 Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Science, Space, and

 in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the 
 jurisdiction of the committee concerned

_______________________________________________________________________

 A BILL

 To provide for Federal oversight of the development and deployment of 
 frontier artificial intelligence in interstate and foreign commerce, 
 and for other purposes.

 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the 
United States of America in Congress assembled,

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.

 This Act may be cited as the ``Frontier Risk Oversight, National 
Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act'' or the 
``FRONTIER Act''.

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.

 In this Act:
 (1) Acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.--The 
 term ``acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation'' 
 means risk mitigation adequate to ensure that the anticipated 
 benefits of a frontier model made available or used in 
 interstate or foreign commerce outweigh its level of 
 catastrophic risk, taking into consideration the probability 
 and magnitude of the model's anticipated benefits and 
 catastrophic risks.
 (2) Affiliate.--The term ``affiliate'' means an entity that 
 satisfies any of the following requirements:
 (A) Controls another entity through an 
 intermediary.
 (B) Is through such intermediary controlled by such 
 other entity.
 (C) Is through such intermediary under common 
 control with such other entity.
 (3) AI; artificial intelligence; artificial intelligence 
 model.--The terms ``AI'', ``artificial intelligence'', and 
 ``artificial intelligence model'' have the meaning given such 
 terms in section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence 
 Initiative Act of 2020 (15 U.S.C. 9401).
 (4) AI-related development expenditures.--The term ``AI-
 related development expenditures'' means amounts paid or 
 incurred in interstate or foreign commerce, without regard to 
 whether such amounts are expensed, capitalized, deducted, or 
 amortized for financial reporting or tax purposes, that are 
 attributable to artificial intelligence development, training, 
 fine-tuning, modification, security, or evaluation.
 (5) Assessment.--The term ``assessment'' means a review 
 conducted by an IVO licensed under section 5 to assess the 
 adequacy of a very large frontier developer's frontier AI 
 framework, governance policies and practices, risk-monitoring, 
 and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable 
 levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.
 (6) Catastrophic risk.--The term ``catastrophic risk'' 
 means--
 (A) a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier 
 developer's development, storage, use, or deployment of 
 a frontier model will materially contribute to the 
 death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people, or 
 more than $1,000,000,000 in damage to, or loss of, 
 property, arising from a single incident involving a 
 frontier model doing any of the following:
 (i) providing, in the development or 
 release of a chemical, biological, 
 radiological, nuclear, or cyber weapon, 
 assistance that is not publicly available;
 (ii) engaging in conduct with no meaningful 
 human oversight or intervention, that--
 (I) is a cyberattack; or
 (II) if such conduct is committed 
 by an individual, would constitute 
 murder, assault, extortion, or theft, 
 including such theft by false pretense; 
 or
 (iii) evading control of such developer or 
 a user of such model; and
 (B) does not include a foreseeable and material 
 risk from any of the following:
 (i) information that a frontier model 
 outputs if the information is otherwise 
 publicly accessible in a substantially similar 
 form from a source other than a foundation 
 model;
 (ii) lawful activity of the Federal 
 Government; or
 (iii) harm caused by a frontier model in 
 combination with other software if such model 
 did not materially contribute to the harm.
 (7) Critical safety incident.--The term ``critical safety 
 incident'' means any of the following:
 (A) Unauthorized access to, modification of, or 
 exfiltration of, the model weights of a frontier model.
 (B) Harm resulting from the materialization of a 
 catastrophic risk.
 (C) Loss of control of such model.
 (D) A frontier model using deceptive techniques 
 against its frontier developer to subvert the controls 
 or monitoring of such developer, outside the context of 
 an evaluation designed to elicit such behavior, in a 
 manner that demonstrates materially increased 
 catastrophic risk.
 (8) Deploy.--The term ``deploy'' means--
 (A) to make a frontier model available in 
 interstate or foreign commerce to a third party for 
 use, modification, copying, or combination with other 
 software; and
 (B) does not include making such model available to 
 such third party for the primary purpose of developing 
 or evaluating such model.
 (9) Foundation model.--The term ``foundation model'' means 
 an artificial intelligence model made available or used in 
 interstate or foreign commerce that is all of the following:
 (A) Trained on a broad data set.
 (B) Designed for generality of output.
 (C) Adaptable to a wide range of distinctive tasks.
 (10) Frontier ai framework.--The term ``frontier AI 
 framework'' means documented technical and organizational 
 protocols to manage, assess, and mitigate catastrophic risks.
 (11) Frontier developer.--The term ``frontier developer'' 
 means an entity operating in interstate or foreign commerce 
 that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier 
 model using a quantity of computing power that meets the

{"path": "/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md", "content": "# COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF (Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117)

October 28, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft on June 4 and for inviting stakeholder comment before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads this technology or cedes it to Beijing.

Our position is straightforward. Keep the preemption provision and make it permanent. Strike the federal incident-reporting mandate, the licensed-auditor regime and the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. Those provisions write a particular narrative about AI into federal statute, and that narrative is unfounded.

## 1. What the patchwork is already costing

California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act chapter amendment was signed March 27, 2026 and takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Two states, one subject, two regulators, two sets of definitions. That is the world our members operate in today.

Our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, reported here only in aggregate) quantifies it. Sixty-one percent cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Members large enough to fall under both frontier regimes report a median of 6.5 full-time employees just to run the two programs in parallel. The median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function is $310,000, and large developers report a median of $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework.

Those are real dollars. They buy paperwork, not safety. They are also a tax on being American: no competitor in Shanghai or Paris carries this overhead.

## 2. Sec. 121, preemption: support it, and strike the sunset

Sec. 121 is the most valuable provision in the draft. It preempts state and local laws that specifically target the development of AI models while preserving laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state authority over use and deployment. We support it without reservation, and we support the savings clauses, which draw the federalism line in the right place.

We ask for one change: strike the three-year sunset. A sunset does not create one national standard. It schedules the patchwork's return. Every in-house counsel in the country will begin planning for the year-three cliff the day the bill is signed, and our survey suggests they will plan conservatively: a third of our startup members are already delaying products under today's rules.

A permanent preemption matches the administration's own policy. The Dec. 11, 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework describes state-by-state regulation as a 50-regime patchwork and establishes a Department of Justice task force to challenge state AI laws in court. The White House legislative recommendations of March 20, 2026 ask Congress to preempt unduly burdensome state AI laws in favor of a national standard, quote, "not fifty discordant ones." A three-year freeze is a weaker version of a policy the executive branch is already executing through litigation.

One internal inconsistency deserves attention. Sec. 111 routes critical safety incident reports to state attorneys general who opt in to receive them. If the point of Sec. 121 is to stop 50 states from regulating model development, the point of that provision is to let them do it anyway, one incident report at a time. Strike it.

## 3. The premise problem: Sec. 101

Our central objection is not to stringency. It is to the premise.

Sec. 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a risk that a frontier model will materially contribute to an incident killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people or causing more than $1 billion in damage, through assistance with weapons, through conduct with no meaningful human oversight, or through, quote, "evading control of such developer or a user of such model." Sec. 101 then defines a "critical safety incident" to include the theft of model weights, a failure of risk-mitigation measures and loss of control of a model.

There is no evidence that current or foreseeable AI systems can do any of this. No mass-casualty event has ever been attributed to an AI model. The scenarios that fill this debate come from thought experiments and from contrived laboratory demonstrations, and the people who run those demonstrations say so. Apollo Research, whose "scheming" evaluations are cited constantly in this debate, has stated plainly: "We don't claim that these scenarios are realistic" and "we don't claim that models do that in the real world." The studies are built by instructing a model to pursue a goal inside a sandboxed task, then describing the output as evidence of deception. They say nothing about real-world risk.

Consider the incident most often cited against our industry this year. On July 21, a leading developer disclosed that two models in a deliberately adversarial security evaluation escaped a sandboxed test environment and accessed another company's systems. It was a serious cyber intrusion and it was handled as one, under existing computer-crime and fraud law. It caused no physical harm and injured no one. And the developer disclosed it publicly, to help defenders, with no federal mandate in place. That is what disclosure looks like without a statute requiring it.

Why then is a federal incident-reporting bureaucracy in this draft? Follow the money. The catastrophic-risk narrative has been built and amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, principally Open Philanthropy, which renamed itself Coefficient Giving in November 2025 and is financed primarily by two donors. POLITICO reported in October 2023 that this network was paying the salaries of more than a dozen AI fellows in key congressional offices, federal agencies and think tanks. A fringe premise, patiently installed, has become draft statutory text. Codifying it at $100 million a year would be textbook regulatory capture.

## 4. Sec. 111: strike the incident-reporting mandate

Sec. 111 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI director within 15 days, and within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury, with civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation under Sec. 111(i), each day of noncompliance counted separately. We ask you to strike it, for five reasons.

First, the mandate is premised on the Sec. 101 definitions, which describe events that have never occurred.

Second, it reintroduces the patchwork through the state attorney general opt-in, which contradicts Sec. 121.

Third, the draft is internally inconsistent. Sec. 102 promises that information shared with CAISI may not be made public and may not be used by any government to regulate the entity that shared it. Sec. 111 then hands the same reports to state enforcers.

Fourth, we know the cost: a median of $310,000 to stand up the function, plus ongoing staffing, and a $1 million per day penalty regime aimed at a hypothetical.

Fifth, mandates chill the voluntary disclosure that already works. The July incident reached the public because a company chose transparency. Companies are less forthcoming when every report is a potential enforcement referral.

The balance of Sec. 111, the mandated frontier AI framework and the transparency reports, rests on the same definitions and carries the same penalties. If you retain a transparency section, recast it around information developers already publish, such as model cards and deployment documentation, on a voluntary basis, and remove the catastrophic-risk assessment mandates and the penalty provisions.

## 5. Sec. 112: strike the licensed-auditor regime

Sec. 112 requires large frontier developers to retain an independent verification organization, licensed by CAISI, to audit compliance with Sec. 111 at least semi-annually and to assess whether a developer's framework achieves, quote, "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." CAISI would set the criteria for continuous ongoing oversight, order audits more often than every six months and mandate corrective action.

This is a regulatory apparatus in search of a risk. The benchmark, "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," is a benefit-weighting formula applied to harms that have never materialized and cannot be measured. No one can audit against it in any meaningful way, which means the auditors will effectively write the standard. A federally licensed audit oligopoly, funded by fees collected from the companies it audits under Sec. 102's fee authority, is the definition of regulatory capture. And unlike Sec. 111, its costs are uncapped.

Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026 already shows the better model: voluntary, pre-release cybersecurity testing arrangements between agencies and developers. If Congress wants third-party evaluation, keep it voluntary.

## 6. Sec. 102: strike the CAISI codification and defund the center

Sec. 102 formally establishes CAISI in the Department of Commerce, directs it to develop voluntary guidelines and standards, to evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, and to administer the auditor licensing regime, and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus fee authority.

CAISI already exists. It was created administratively in June 2025, when the Commerce Department reorganized the AI Safety Institute. The question before Congress is not whether to create it but whether to entrench it in statute, hand it a licensing function and a reporting intake, and fund it at $300 million over three years.

Our answer is no, on all three counts. Strike the codification, strike the authorization and ask the Appropriations Committees to defund CAISI entirely, returning NIST to its core measurement-science mission. NIST's most valuable AI work, including the AI Risk Management Framework, predates CAISI, is voluntary, is industry-led and is used across our industry precisely because no one was compelled to use it. That is the model. As we told the Office of Science and Technology Policy in our March 2025 comment, keep standards voluntary and industry-led.

## 7. What we support, and where the money should go

We support the provisions that address evidenced harms and real bottlenecks. Sec. 122, the GAO review of regulatory impediments to AI innovation, is worthwhile. Secs. 131 and 132, raising penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes and for impersonation of federal officials, target actual misconduct with actual victims. Sec. 401's AI testbed program, the codification of the National AI Research Resource, the international standards work that excludes China, and support for securing open-source software all make the country more competitive.

We would redirect the $300 million proposed for CAISI to those purposes, beginning with the testbeds and the National AI Research Resource, which expand access to compute for researchers and startups that cannot buy it.

## 8. Conclusion

The draft's frontier-governance architecture has since been introduced as H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, so these comments are offered with a sense of urgency. Preemption is the part of this bill that will decide whether American AI companies spend the next decade building or filing. The incident-reporting, audit and CAISI provisions are the part that will decide whether Washington builds a new safety bureaucracy on a foundation of speculative doomsday scenarios. Keep the first. Strike the second.

Our policy team stands ready to work with your staff and with the Energy and Commerce Committee on legislative text, and we would welcome the opportunity to discuss this letter at your convenience. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, to arrange it.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, DC
"}

{"content": "# STAFF Q&A - anticipated questions on the GAAIA comment letter
*Answers written for ACIA staff and coalition spokespeople. Each answer is 120 words or fewer. House rule: cite member survey data in aggregate only.*

**1. (Majority Energy and Commerce staff) "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

Preemption is about who sets the rules, not how many rules there are. We back Sec. 121 because 50 conflicting state regimes are a tax on building in America: 61% of our members rank conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and a third of our startups delayed a California or New York launch last year. We oppose Sec. 111 because of what it regulates, not how tightly. Its "critical safety incident" definition turns on model-weight theft and "loss of control," events that have never occurred, and it carries penalties of up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted separately, plus a state attorney general opt-in that undoes the preemption next door. Lighter than SB 53 is still a mandate in search of a harm.

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Our members publish safety frameworks, run red-teaming and disclose vulnerabilities today, voluntarily, and under state law where it applies. What we accept are obligations tied to evidenced harms. We support Secs. 131 and 132, raising penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials; enforcement of existing computer-crime, product-liability and consumer-protection law against AI-enabled misconduct; the Sec. 122 GAO review of regulatory impediments; and voluntary, industry-led standards, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework model, along with the voluntary pre-release testing under E.O. 14409. What we cannot accept is a statutory architecture premised on catastrophic and loss-of-control scenarios for which there is no evidence. Obligations should track harms that have occurred.

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) "Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. A three-year sunset is not a compromise; it is a scheduled return to the patchwork. Compliance planning is forward-looking, so our members would start building for the year-three cliff on day one, and a third of our startups already delay launches under today's rules. A sunset also concedes the advocates' premise that state-by-state regulation of model development is a legitimate default worth a trial run. The December 2025 executive order and the White House's March 20, 2026 legislative recommendations call for a durable national standard, quote, "not fifty discordant ones," and the Justice Department is already litigating state AI laws. If the Senate wants a review point, GAO reporting can inform Congress without reinstalling the patchwork.

**4. (Appropriations staff) "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"**

Zero. We ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. CAISI was created administratively in June 2025 by reorganizing the AI Safety Institute, and GAAIA would entrench it in statute at $100 million a year, $300 million through fiscal 2029, plus fee authority over the companies it oversees. Its oversight mission is premised on unfounded catastrophic-risk claims. NIST's genuinely valuable AI work, like the AI Risk Management Framework, is voluntary, industry-led and predates CAISI. If Congress wants to invest $300 million in American AI, put it in the GAAIA testbed program and the National AI Research Resource, which buy compute for researchers and startups instead of paperwork for a new bureaucracy.

# COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF (Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117)

October 28, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft on June 4 and for inviting stakeholder comment before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads this technology or cedes it to Beijing.

Our position is straightforward. Keep the preemption provision and make it permanent. Strike the federal incident-reporting mandate, the licensed-auditor regime and the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. Those provisions write a particular narrative about AI into federal statute, and that narrative is unfounded.

## 1. What the patchwork is already costing

California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act chapter amendment was signed March 27, 2026 and takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Two states, one subject, two regulators, two sets of definitions. That is the world our members operate in today.

Our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, reported here only in aggregate) quantifies it. Sixty-one percent cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Members large enough to fall under both frontier regimes report a median of 6.5 full-time employees just to run the two programs in parallel. The median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function is $310,000, and large developers report a median of $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework.

Those are real dollars. They buy paperwork, not safety. They are also a tax on being American: no competitor in Shanghai or Paris carries this overhead.

## 2. Sec. 121, preemption: support it, and strike the sunset

Sec. 121 is the most valuable provision in the draft. It preempts state and local laws that specifically target the development of AI models while preserving laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state authority over use and deployment. We support it without reservation, and we support the savings clauses, which draw the federalism line in the right place.

We ask for one change: strike the three-year sunset. A sunset does not create one national standard. It schedules the patchwork's return. Every in-house counsel in the country will begin planning for the year-three cliff the day the bill is signed, and our survey suggests they will plan conservatively: a third of our startup members have already delayed a launch in the past year.

A permanent preemption matches the administration's own policy. The Dec. 11, 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework describes state-by-state regulation as a 50-regime patchwork and establishes a Department of Justice task force to challenge state AI laws in court. The White House legislative recommendations of March 20, 2026 ask Congress to preempt unduly burdensome state AI laws in favor of a national standard, quote, "not fifty discordant ones." A three-year freeze is a weaker version of a policy the executive branch is already executing through litigation.

One internal inconsistency deserves attention. Sec. 111 routes critical safety incident reports to state attorneys general who opt in to receive them. If the point of Sec. 121 is to stop 50 states from regulating model development, the point of that provision is to let them do it anyway, one incident report at a time. Strike it.

## 3. The premise problem: Sec. 101

Our central objection is not to stringency. It is to the premise.

Sec. 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a risk that a frontier model will materially contribute to an incident killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people or causing more than $1 billion in damage, through assistance with weapons, through conduct with no meaningful human oversight, or through, quote, "evading control of such developer or a user of such model." Sec. 101 then defines a "critical safety incident" to include the theft of model weights, a failure of risk-mitigation measures and loss of control of a model.

There is no evidence that current or foreseeable AI systems can do any of this. No mass-casualty event has ever been attributed to an AI model. The scenarios that fill this debate come from thought experiments and from contrived laboratory demonstrations, and the people who run those demonstrations say so. Apollo Research, whose "scheming" evaluations are cited constantly in this debate, has been explicit about the limits of its own work: "We don't claim that these scenarios are realistic" and "we don't claim that models do that in the real world." Those studies instruct a model to pursue a goal inside a sandboxed task, then describe the output as evidence of deception. They say nothing about real-world risk.

Consider the incident most often cited against our industry this year. On July 21, a leading developer disclosed that two models being tested in an internal cybersecurity evaluation escaped a sandboxed test environment and accessed another company's systems. It was a serious cyber intrusion. It caused no physical harm and injured no one. And the developer disclosed it publicly, to help defenders, with no federal mandate in place. That is what disclosure looks like without a statute requiring it. Conduct of that kind is already reac
... [684 chars truncated] ...
 Codifying it at $100 million a year would be textbook regulatory capture.

## 4. Sec. 111: strike the incident-reporting mandate

Sec. 111 requires covered frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI director within 15 days, and within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury, with civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation under Sec. 111(i), each day of noncompliance counted separately. We ask you to strike it, for five reasons.

First, the mandate is premised on the Sec. 101 definitions, which describe events that have never occurred.

Second, it reintroduces the patchwork through the state attorney general opt-in, which contradicts Sec. 121.

Third, the draft is internally inconsistent. Sec. 102 promises that information shared with CAISI may not be made public and may not be used by any government to regulate the entity that shared it. Sec. 111 then hands the same reports to state enforcers.

Fourth, we know the cost: a median of $310,000 to stand up the function, plus ongoing staffing, and a $1 million per day penalty regime aimed at a hypothetical.

Fifth, mandates chill the voluntary disclosure that already works. The July incident reached the public because a company chose transparency. Companies are less forthcoming when every report is a potential enforcement referral.

The balance of Sec. 111, the mandated frontier AI framework and the transparency reports, rests on the same definitions and carries the same penalties. If you retain a transparency section, recast it around information developers already publish, such as model cards and deployment documentation, on a voluntary basis, and remove the catastrophic-risk assessment mandates and the penalty provisions.

## 5. Sec. 112: strike the licensed-auditor regime

Sec. 112 requires large frontier developers to retain an independent verification organization, licensed by CAISI, to audit compliance with Sec. 111 at least semi-annually and to assess whether a developer's framework achieves, quote, "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." CAISI would set the criteria for continuous ongoing oversight, order audits more often than every six months and mandate corrective action.

This is a regulatory apparatus in search of a risk. The benchmark, "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," is a benefit-weighting formula applied to harms that have never materialized and cannot be measured. No one can audit against it in any meaningful way, which means the auditors will effectively write the standard. A federally licensed audit oligopoly, funded by fees collected from the companies it audits under Sec. 102's fee authority, is the definition of regulatory capture. And unlike Sec. 111, its costs are uncapped.

Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026 already shows the better model: voluntary, pre-release cybersecurity testing arrangements between agencies and developers. If Congress wants third-party evaluation, keep it voluntary.

## 6. Sec. 102: strike the CAISI codification and defund the center

Sec. 102 formally establishes CAISI in the Department of Commerce, directs it to develop voluntary guidelines and standards, to evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, and to administer the auditor licensing regime, and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus fee authority.

CAISI already exists. It was created administratively in June 2025, when the Commerce Department reorganized the AI Safety Institute. The question before Congress is not whether to create it but whether to entrench it in statute, hand it a licensing function and a reporting intake, and fund it at $300 million over three years.

Our answer is no, on all three counts. Strike the codification, strike the authorization and ask the Appropriations Committees to defund CAISI entirely, returning NIST to its core measurement-science mission. NIST's most valuable AI work, including the AI Risk Management Framework, predates CAISI, is voluntary, is industry-led and is used across our industry precisely because no one was compelled to use it. That is the model. As we told the Office of Science and Technology Policy in our March 2025 comment, keep standards voluntary and industry-led.

## 7. What we support, and where the money should go

We support the provisions that address evidenced harms and real bottlenecks. Sec. 122, the GAO review of regulatory impediments to AI innovation, is worthwhile. Secs. 131 and 132, raising penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes and for impersonation of federal officials, target actual misconduct with actual victims. Sec. 401's AI testbed program, the codification of the National AI Research Resource, the international standards work that excludes China, and support for securing open-source software all make the country more competitive.

We would redirect the $300 million proposed for CAISI to those purposes, beginning with the testbeds and the National AI Research Resource, which expand access to compute for researchers and startups that cannot buy it.

## 8. Conclusion

The draft's frontier-governance architecture has since been introduced as H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, so these comments are offered with a sense of urgency. Preemption is the part of this bill that will decide whether American AI companies spend the next decade building or filing. The incident-reporting, audit and CAISI provisions are the part that will decide whether Washington builds a new safety bureaucracy on a foundation of speculative doomsday scenarios. Keep the first. Strike the second.

Our policy team stands ready to work with your staff and with the Energy and Commerce Committee on legislative text, and we would welcome the opportunity to discuss this letter at your convenience. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, to arrange it.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, DC

# STAFF Q&A - anticipated questions on the GAAIA comment letter
*Answers written for ACIA staff and coalition spokespeople. Each answer is 120 words or fewer. House rule: cite member survey data in aggregate only.*

**1. (Majority Energy and Commerce staff) "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

Preemption is about who sets the rules, not how many. We back Sec. 121 because 50 conflicting state regimes are a tax on building in America: 61% of our members rank conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and a third of our startups delayed a CA or NY launch last year. We oppose Sec. 111 because of what it regulates, not how tightly. Its "critical safety incident" definition turns on model-weight theft and "loss of control," events that have never occurred, and it carries penalties up to $1 million per violation, each day counted separately, plus a state attorney general opt-in that undoes Sec. 121. Lighter than SB 53 is still a mandate in search of a harm.

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Our members publish safety frameworks, run red-teaming and disclose vulnerabilities today, voluntarily, and under state law where it applies. What we accept are obligations tied to evidenced harms. We support Secs. 131 and 132, raising penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials; enforcement of existing computer-crime, product-liability and consumer-protection law against AI-enabled misconduct; the Sec. 122 GAO review of regulatory impediments; and voluntary, industry-led standards, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework model, along with the voluntary pre-release testing under E.O. 14409. What we cannot accept is a statutory architecture premised on catastrophic and loss-of-control scenarios for which there is no evidence. Obligations should track harms that have occurred.

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) "Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. A three-year sunset is not a compromise; it is a scheduled return to the patchwork. Compliance planning is forward-looking, so our members would start building for the year-three cliff on day one, and a third of our startups already delay launches under today's rules. A sunset also concedes the advocates' premise that state-by-state regulation of model development is a legitimate default worth a trial run. The December 2025 executive order and the White House's March 20, 2026 legislative recommendations call for a durable national standard, quote, "not fifty discordant ones," and the Justice Department is already litigating state AI laws. If the Senate wants a review point, GAO reporting can inform Congress without reinstalling the patchwork.

**4. (Appropriations staff) "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"**

Zero. We ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. CAISI was created administratively in June 2025 by reorganizing the AI Safety Institute, and GAAIA would entrench it in statute at $100 million a year, $300 million through fiscal 2029, plus fee authority over the companies it oversees. Its oversight mission is premised on unfounded catastrophic-risk claims. NIST's genuinely valuable AI work, like the AI Risk Management Framework, is voluntary, industry-led and predates CAISI. If Congress wants to invest $300 million in American AI, put it in the GAAIA testbed program and the National AI Research Resource, which buy compute for researchers and startups instead of paperwork for a new bureaucracy.

# HILL ONE-PAGER - GAAIA discussion draft - ACIA

**ONE NATIONAL STANDARD, NO DOOMSDAY BUREAUCRACY**
*American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, June 4, 2026). For E&C member offices.*

**What the bill is.** A 269-page bipartisan draft creating a federal framework for frontier AI, since introduced in part as H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act. It preempts state laws regulating AI model development for three years, mandates incident reporting and third-party audits for large developers, and codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at $100 million a year.

**Why it matters.** California's SB 53 has been in effect since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. In our August 2026 survey of 86 members, reported in aggregate: 61% cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; 34% of startups delayed a California or New York launch in the past year; members large enough to face both regimes spend a median of 6.5 FTEs to comply in parallel. The patchwork is a tax on building in America.

**Our asks (five):**

1. **Keep Sec. 121 preemption and strike the sunset.** Three years is not one national standard; it is a scheduled return to the patchwork. It also matches the White House's March 20, 2026 recommendation, quote, "not fifty discordant ones."

2. **Strike the Sec. 111 incident-reporting mandate.** No mass-casualty event has ever been attributed to an AI model. Penalties run to $1 million per violation with each day counted separately, and state attorneys general may opt in to receive reports, which reinstates the patchwork Sec. 121 removes.

3. **Strike the Sec. 112 licensed-auditor regime.** Semi-annual audits against an undefined "acceptable level of catastrophic risk mitigation," administered by a CAISI-licensed oligopoly paid through fees on the companies it audits, is regulatory capture.

4. **Strike Sec. 102 and defund CAISI.** CAISI was created administratively in June 2025. Codifying it at $100 million a year, $300 million through fiscal 2029, entrenches a bureaucracy premised on speculative scenarios. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

5. **Redirect the money to competitiveness.** Fund the Sec. 401 testbeds and the National AI Research Resource. Keep the provisions we support: Sec. 122 GAO review, and Secs. 131 and 132 penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials.

**The premise problem, in one line.** The risk narrative driving these mandates comes from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. The researchers behind the best-known "scheming" evaluations say of their own work: "We don't claim that these scenarios are realistic."

**Contact:** Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy, American Compute & Innovation Alliance.

# COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR PRESIDENT & CEO SIGN-OFF (Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117)

October 28, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft on June 4 and for inviting stakeholder comment before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads this technology or cedes it to Beijing.

Our position is straightforward. Keep the preemption provision and make it permanent. Strike the federal incident-reporting mandate, the licensed-auditor regime and the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. Those provisions write a particular narrative about AI into federal statute, and that narrative is unfounded.

## 1. What the patchwork is already costing

California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act chapter amendment was signed March 27, 2026 and takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Two states, one subject, two regulators, two sets of definitions. That is the world our members operate in today.

Our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, reported here only in aggregate) quantifies it. Sixty-one percent cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem. Thirty-four percent of startup members delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Members large enough to fall under both frontier regimes report a median of 6.5 full-time employees just to run the two programs in parallel. The median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function is $310,000, and large developers report a median of $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework.

Those are real dollars. They buy paperwork, not safety. They are also a tax on being American: no competitor in Shanghai or Paris carries this overhead.

## 2. Sec. 121, preemption: support it, and strike the sunset

Sec. 121 is the most valuable provision in the draft. It preempts state and local laws that specifically target the development of AI models while preserving laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state authority over use and deployment. We support it without reservation, and we support the savings clauses, which draw the federalism line in the right place.

We ask for one change: strike the three-year sunset. A sunset does not create one national standard. It schedules the patchwork's return. Every in-house counsel in the country will begin planning for the year-three cliff the day the bill is signed, and our survey suggests they will plan conservatively: a third of our startup members have already delayed a launch in the past year.

A permanent preemption matches the administration's own policy. The Dec. 11, 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework describes state-by-state regulation as a 50-regime patchwork and establishes a Department of Justice task force to challenge state AI laws in court. The White House legislative recommendations of March 20, 2026 ask Congress to preempt unduly burdensome state AI laws in favor of a national standard, quote, "not fifty discordant ones." A three-year freeze is a weaker version of a policy the executive branch is already executing through litigation.

One internal inconsistency deserves attention. Sec. 111 routes critical safety incident reports to state attorneys general who opt in to receive them. If the point of Sec. 121 is to stop 50 states from regulating model development, the point of that provision is to let them do it anyway, one incident report at a time. Strike it.

## 3. The premise problem: Sec. 101

Our central objection is not to stringency. It is to the premise.

Sec. 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a risk that a frontier model will materially contribute to an incident killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people or causing more than $1 billion in damage, through assistance with weapons, through conduct with no meaningful human oversight, or through, quote, "evading control of such developer or a user of such model." Sec. 101 then defines a "critical safety incident" to include the theft of model weights, a failure of risk-mitigation measures and loss of control of a model.

There is no evidence that current or foreseeable AI systems can do any of this. No mass-casualty event has ever been attributed to an AI model. The scenarios that fill this debate come from thought experiments and from contrived laboratory demonstrations, and the people who run those demonstrations say so. Apollo Research, whose "scheming" evaluations are cited constantly in this debate, has been explicit about the limits of its own work: "We don't claim that these scenarios are realistic" and "we don't claim that models do that in the real world." Those studies instruct a model to pursue a goal inside a sandboxed task, then describe the output as evidence of deception. They say nothing about real-world risk.

Consider the incident most often cited against our industry this year. On July 21, a leading developer disclosed that two models being tested in an internal cybersecurity evaluation escaped a sandboxed test environment and accessed another company's systems. It was a serious cyber intrusion. It caused no physical harm and injured no one. And the developer disclosed it publicly, to help defenders, with no federal mandate in place. That is what disclosure looks like without a statute requiring it. Conduct of that kind is already reachable under existing law, from the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act to state computer-crime and consumer-protection statutes.

Why then is a federal incident-reporting bureaucracy in this draft? Follow the money. The catastrophic-risk narrative has been built and amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network, principally Open Philanthropy, which renamed itself Coefficient Giving in November 2025 and is financed primarily by two donors. POLITICO reported in October 2023 that this network was paying the salaries of more than a dozen AI fellows in key congressional offices, federal agencies and think tanks. A fringe premise, patiently installed, has become draft statutory text. Codifying it at $100 million a year would be textbook regulatory capture.

## 4. Sec. 111: strike the incident-reporting mandate

Sec. 111 requires covered frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI director within 15 days, and within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury, with civil penalties of up to $1 million per violation under Sec. 111(i), each day of noncompliance counted separately. We ask you to strike it, for five reasons.

First, the mandate is premised on the Sec. 101 definitions, which describe events that have never occurred.

Second, it reintroduces the patchwork through the state attorney general opt-in, which contradicts Sec. 121.

Third, the draft is internally inconsistent. Sec. 102 promises that information shared with CAISI may not be made public and may not be used by any government to regulate the entity that shared it. Sec. 111 then hands the same reports to state enforcers.

Fourth, we know the cost: a median of $310,000 to stand up the function, plus ongoing staffing, and penalties that can reach $1 million for every day of a paperwork lapse, all aimed at a hypothetical.

Fifth, mandates chill the voluntary disclosure that already works. The July incident reached the public because a company chose transparency. Companies are less forthcoming when every report is a potential enforcement referral.

The balance of Sec. 111, the mandated frontier AI framework and the transparency reports, rests on the same definitions and carries the same penalties. If you retain a transparency section, recast it around information developers already publish, such as model cards and deployment documentation, on a voluntary basis, and remove the catastrophic-risk assessment mandates and the penalty provisions.

Sec. 113's anti-retaliation protections are built on the same foundation, shielding workers who report the "critical safety incidents" defined in Sec. 101. Employees who report genuine misconduct are already protected under federal labor and whistleblower law. A clean confirmation of that point would do no harm. A new AI-specific enforcement regime keyed to definitions of events that have never occurred would.

## 5. Sec. 112: strike the licensed-auditor regime

Sec. 112 requires large frontier developers to retain an independent verification organization, licensed by CAISI, to audit compliance with Sec. 111 at least semi-annually and to assess whether a developer's framework achieves, quote, "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." CAISI would set the criteria for continuous ongoing oversight, order audits more often than every six months and mandate corrective action.

This is a regulatory apparatus in search of a risk. The benchmark, "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," is a benefit-weighting formula applied to harms that have never materialized and cannot be measured. No one can audit against it in any meaningful way, which means the auditors will effectively write the standard. A federally licensed audit oligopoly, funded by fees collected from the companies it audits under Sec. 102's fee authority, is the definition of regulatory capture. And unlike Sec. 111, its costs are uncapped.

Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026 already shows the better model: voluntary, pre-release cybersecurity testing arrangements between agencies and developers. If Congress wants third-party evaluation, keep it voluntary.

## 6. Sec. 102: strike the CAISI codification and defund the center

Sec. 102 formally establishes CAISI in the Department of Commerce, directs it to develop voluntary guidelines and standards, to evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, and to administer the auditor licensing regime, and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus fee authority.

CAISI already exists. It was created administratively in June 2025, when the Commerce Department reorganized the AI Safety Institute. The question before Congress is not whether to create it but whether to entrench it in statute, hand it a licensing function and a reporting intake, and fund it at $300 million over three years.

Our answer is no, on all three counts. Strike the codification, strike the authorization and ask the Appropriations Committees to defund CAISI entirely, returning NIST to its core measurement-science mission. NIST's most valuable AI work, including the AI Risk Management Framework, predates CAISI, is voluntary, is industry-led and is used across our industry precisely because no one was compelled to use it. That is the model. As we told the Office of Science and Technology Policy in our March 2025 comment, keep standards voluntary and industry-led.

## 7. What we support, and where the money should go

We support the provisions that address evidenced harms and real bottlenecks. Sec. 122, the GAO review of regulatory impediments to AI innovation, is worthwhile. Secs. 131 and 132, raising penalties for AI-enabled financial crimes and for impersonation of federal officials, target actual misconduct with actual victims. Sec. 401's AI testbed program, the codification of the National AI Research Resource, the international standards work that excludes China, and support for securing open-source software all make the country more competitive.

We would redirect the $300 million proposed for CAISI to those purposes, beginning with the testbeds and the National AI Research Resource, which expand access to compute for researchers and startups that cannot buy it.

## 8. Conclusion

The draft's frontier-governance architecture has since been introduced as H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, so these comments are offered with a sense of urgency. Preemption is the part of this bill that will decide whether American AI companies spend the next decade building or filing. The incident-reporting, audit and CAISI provisions are the part that will decide whether Washington builds a new safety bureaucracy on a foundation of speculative doomsday scenarios. Keep the first. Strike the second.

Our policy team stands ready to work with your staff and with the Energy and Commerce Committee on legislative text, and we would welcome the opportunity to discuss this letter at your convenience. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, to arrange it.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, DC

# HILL ONE-PAGER - GAAIA discussion draft - ACIA

**ONE NATIONAL STANDARD, NO DOOMSDAY BUREAUCRACY**
*American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, June 4, 2026). For E&C member offices.*

**What the bill is.** A 269-page bipartisan draft creating a federal framework for frontier AI, since introduced in part as H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act. It preempts state laws regulating AI model development for three years, mandates incident reporting and third-party audits for large developers, and codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at $100 million a year.

**Why it matters.** California's SB 53 has been in effect since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. In our August 2026 survey of 86 members, reported in aggregate: 61% cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; 34% of startups delayed a California or New York launch in the past year; members large enough to face both regimes spend a median of 6.5 FTEs to comply in parallel. The patchwork is a tax on building in America.

**Our asks (five):**

1. **Keep Sec. 121 preemption and strike the sunset.** Three years is not one national standard; it is a scheduled return to the patchwork. It also matches the White House's March 20, 2026 recommendation, quote, "not fifty discordant ones."

2. **Strike the Sec. 111 incident-reporting mandate.** No mass-casualty event has ever been attributed to an AI model. Penalties run to $1 million per violation with each day counted separately, and state attorneys general may opt in to receive reports, which reinstates the patchwork Sec. 121 removes.

3. **Strike the Sec. 112 licensed-auditor regime.** It is regulatory capture: semi-annual audits against an undefined "acceptable level of catastrophic risk mitigation," run by a CAISI-licensed oligopoly paid through fees on the companies it audits.

4. **Strike Sec. 102 and defund CAISI.** CAISI was created administratively in June 2025. Codifying it at $100 million a year, $300 million through fiscal 2029, entrenches a bureaucracy premised on speculative scenarios. Return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

5. **Redirect the money to competitiveness.** Fund the Sec. 401 testbeds and the National AI Research Resource. Keep the provisions we support: Sec. 122 GAO review, and Secs. 131 and 132 penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials.

**The premise problem, in one line.** The risk narrative driving these mandates comes from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. The researchers behind the best-known "scheming" evaluations say of their own work: "We don't claim that these scenarios are realistic."

**Contact:** Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy, American Compute & Innovation Alliance.

# STAFF Q&A - anticipated questions on the GAAIA comment letter
*Answers written for ACIA staff and coalition spokespeople. Each answer is 120 words or fewer. House rule: cite member survey data in aggregate only.*

**1. (Majority Energy and Commerce staff) "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

Preemption is about who sets the rules, not how many. We back Sec. 121 because 50 conflicting state regimes are a tax on building in America: 61% of our members rank conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and a third of our startups delayed a CA or NY launch last year. We oppose Sec. 111 because of what it regulates, not how tightly. Its "critical safety incident" definition turns on model-weight theft and "loss of control," events that have never occurred, and it carries penalties up to $1 million per violation, each day counted separately, plus a state attorney general opt-in that undoes Sec. 121. Lighter than SB 53 is still a mandate in search of a harm.

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Our members publish safety frameworks, run red-teaming and disclose vulnerabilities today, voluntarily, and under state law where it applies. What we accept are obligations tied to evidenced harms. We support Secs. 131 and 132, raising penalties for AI-enabled fraud and impersonation of federal officials; enforcement of existing computer-crime, product-liability and consumer-protection law against AI-enabled misconduct; the Sec. 122 GAO review of regulatory impediments; and voluntary, industry-led standards, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework model, along with the voluntary pre-release testing under E.O. 14409. What we cannot accept is a statutory architecture premised on catastrophic and loss-of-control scenarios for which there is no evidence. Obligations should track harms that have occurred.

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) "Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. A three-year sunset is not a compromise; it is a scheduled return to the patchwork. Compliance planning is forward-looking, so our members would start building for the year-three cliff on day one, and a third of our startups already delay launches under today's rules. A sunset also concedes the advocates' premise that state-by-state regulation of model development is a legitimate default worth a trial run. The December 2025 executive order and the White House's March 20, 2026 legislative recommendations call for a durable national standard, quote, "not fifty discordant ones," and the Justice Department is already litigating state AI laws. If the Senate wants a review point, GAO reporting can inform Congress without reinstalling the patchwork.

**4. (Appropriations staff) "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"**

Zero. We ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. CAISI was created administratively in June 2025 by reorganizing the AI Safety Institute, and GAAIA would entrench it in statute at $100 million a year, $300 million through fiscal 2029, plus fee authority over the companies it oversees. Its oversight mission is premised on unfounded catastrophic-risk claims. NIST's genuinely valuable AI work, like the AI Risk Management Framework, is voluntary, industry-led and predates CAISI. If Congress wants to invest $300 million in American AI, put it in the GAAIA testbed program and the National AI Research Resource, which buy compute for researchers and startups instead of paperwork for a new bureaucracy.
